title: Safe changes and long histories

story: Wednesday. The team adds the grill step: before Nova writes a plan, it may ask the requester a few questions. You add one activity call at the top of ticketToPr, the tests pass, and you deploy at 14:00. At that moment twelve runs are open, and RH-1234 has been waiting since Monday for you to approve its plan.

At 14:05 you finally press Approve. The new worker replays RH-1234's history with the new code. The new code asks for the grill first, but the history says the first step was writing the plan. RH-1234 stops moving, and the worker logs a line that starts with [TMPRL1100] Nondeterminism error. So do the other eleven runs, one by one, as each of them gets its next signal or timer.
hook.question: How do you change a workflow's code while runs that started on the old code are still open?

read.h: Why a new step breaks an old run
p: Remember how replay works: a worker runs the workflow from the top and answers every finished step from the history. While it does that, it also checks the code against the history. Each await on an activity, a timer or a condition with a timeout is a command, a request to the Temporal Service, and the commands must come in the same order as the events the history recorded. If the code asks for grill where the history says writePlan was scheduled, the worker cannot know what is true, so it refuses to continue. That refusal is a non-determinism error.

The run does not fail and is not lost. It stays open, and the worker retries it again and again, failing each time, until a worker with compatible code arrives. So the damage is a stuck run, not a broken one, and the fix is in the code.

The rule for what breaks is about commands, not about lines of code. Adding, removing or reordering activity calls, timers or waits before the point an open run has reached breaks it. Changing the code inside an activity is safe, because activity code is never replayed; only its recorded result is used. So are new log lines and renamed variables.
read.see:
WARN temporalio_sdk_core::worker::workflow: Failing workflow task
  [TMPRL1100] Nondeterminism error: Activity type of scheduled event 'writePlan'
  does not match activity type of activity command 'grill'
(trimmed)

deeper.h: Go deeper: running old and new code side by side
p: Temporal has a second way to change workflows, called Worker Deployments. Every worker says which build it runs, and a run can be pinned to the build it started on, so old runs never meet new code. The price is that the old workers must keep running until the last old run closes, which for us can be more than two weeks, because a PR can wait 14 days for its review.
That is why our platform uses patching, which you learn next, together with a replay test in CI. Worker Deployments stay an option for a rewrite that is too big to patch.

read.h: patched(): two paths in one file
p: patched lets the old and the new code live in one file. You wrap the new step in if (patched("grill-step")), where grill-step is an ID you choose for this change. When a run reaches that line for the first time, patched returns true and also writes a marker into the history. When a worker replays a history that has the marker, patched returns true again. When it replays an older history without the marker, it returns false. So RH-1234, which started on Monday, skips the grill and continues with the plan it already has, and every run that starts after the deploy asks its questions first.
Give the ID a name that says what changed, and never use the same ID for a second change. A run that has the marker from the first change would take the second change's path too.

notes.text: True for runs that reach this line after the deploy; false when replaying a history from before it.
The new step: up to five questions to the requester before the plan.
Everything after the patch is the same for old and new runs.

read.see:
$ temporal workflow show -w nova:RH-1235 | grep -v WorkflowTask      (a run started after the deploy)
    1  WorkflowExecutionStarted
    5  MarkerRecorded                   ← patched("grill-step") said true, and wrote it down
    6  UpsertWorkflowSearchAttributes   ← the patch ID is also saved as a search attribute
    9  ActivityTaskCompleted            ← grill
   15  ActivityTaskCompleted            ← writePlan

read.h: Removing a patch, in two more deploys
p: A patch is temporary, and removing it takes care, because the old path is still needed by any run that started before the patch. So a patch lives through three deploys. Deploy 1 adds patched. When no run that started before deploy 1 is still open, deploy 2 replaces it with deprecatePatch, which keeps writing the marker but always takes the new path. When no run that started before deploy 2 is still open, deploy 3 deletes the line, and the code is plain again.

You find old runs with a list query on their start time, for example ExecutionStatus='Running' AND StartTime < '2026-10-14T14:00:00Z'. Our runs can wait up to 14 days for a PR review, so a patch usually lives for about two weeks. And you do not want to learn about a forgotten patch from a stuck run: a replay test in CI, the topic of the next lesson, replays saved histories with the new code before every merge.

notes.text: deprecatePatch keeps the marker, so a run started after deploy 1 still replays cleanly.

read.h: A run that never ends needs a fresh history
p: Long lives cause a second problem: the history itself. A ticket run ends after days, so its history stays small. But one of our workflows never ends: slots, which hands out the VM slots of one agent, for example the three that Nova may use at once. Every request and every release adds events to its history, and a history cannot grow forever. Temporal stops a run whose history reaches 51,200 events or 50 MB, and a long history also makes every replay slower.

continueAsNew solves this. It ends the current run and starts a new run with the same workflow ID and an empty history, and the only things that carry over are the arguments you pass. So slots counts its own history and, once it has 5,000 events, continues as new with the current holders and the waiting line as arguments. To everyone who sends it signals, it is still slots:nova.

notes.text: workflowInfo().historyLength is the number of events so far. 5,000 keeps the history far below the limits.
A new run of slots:<agent> with an empty history, which starts with the same holders and the same waiting line.

lab.title: Break an open run, then patch it
needs: The p7-1 lab folder, for worker.mjs and start.mjs
lab.goal: Deploy a new step while a run is waiting, see the non-determinism error, and fix it with patched so the old run finishes on the old path and new runs take the new one.

guess.q: nova:RH-1234 wrote its plan and is waiting for approval. You add await grill(ticket) before writePlan, restart the worker and approve the run. What happens to RH-1234?

options.text: It runs grill now, then continues and opens the PR.
options.why: The history says writePlan came first. The worker cannot fit grill into a history that already went past that point.

options.text: It fails, and you must start it again from the beginning.
options.why: It does not fail. It stays open and keeps retrying, which is why a fix in the code can still save it.

options.text: It stops moving: the worker reports a non-determinism error and keeps retrying until the code matches the history again.
options.why: Replay found a command (schedule grill) that does not match the recorded event (writePlan scheduled), so it refuses to continue.

follow.say: Start from an empty board, because runs left open by earlier labs would be replayed with this lab's code. The dev server keeps everything in memory, so stop it with Ctrl+C and start it again.

lab.build: Do deploy 2 of the patch. First prove that no run from before your patched deploy is open: temporal workflow list --query "ExecutionStatus='Running' AND StartTime < '<the time of your patched deploy>'" must print no runs (temporal workflow show gives you the times). Then replace the if (patched(...)) block with deprecatePatch('grill-step') followed by a plain await grill(ticket), and add deprecatePatch to the import. Restart the worker, approve RH-1235 so it finishes, and start RH-1236.
checks: After the careless deploy, the worker logged [TMPRL1100] Nondeterminism error and nova:RH-1234 stayed Running.
After the patched deploy, RH-1234 completed with "approved by sean" and never printed a grill line.
RH-1235's history shows MarkerRecorded, and its first line in the worker tab is the grill.
For your build: the list query for old runs printed nothing, RH-1235 completed with deprecatePatch in place, and RH-1236 printed the grill line first.
lab.fix: A teammate saw patched in the code on the day it shipped and thought it was clutter, so they replaced it with a plain await grill(ticket). But RH-1300 had started on version 1 that morning and was still waiting for its approval. Replay it: write version 1 again, restart the worker, start RH-1300 with node start.mjs RH-1300, then stop the worker, write the teammate's plain version 2, start the worker and approve RH-1300. The non-determinism error is back. Put the patch back so RH-1300 finishes, and explain to the teammate when the line can really go.
explain: Why did adding one activity call break a run that was only waiting for an approval?
How does patched know which path a run should take, both the first time and during a replay?
When is it safe to replace patched with deprecatePatch, and when is it safe to delete the line?
lab.done: An open run survived a code change thanks to patched, a new run took the new path with a marker in its history, and you stopped the worker and the dev server.

check.q: Which change to ticketToPr can break runs that are already open?

options.text: Changing the text that the writePlan activity posts to Slack
options.why: That is code inside an activity. Activity code is never replayed; only its recorded result is used.

options.text: Adding an activity call before a point that open runs have already passed
options.why: On replay the new code asks for a step the history does not have, so the worker reports a non-determinism error.

options.text: Renaming a local variable in the workflow
options.why: Names do not appear in the history. Only commands do: activities, timers and other requests to the service.

check.q: A run started before the deploy reaches if (patched("grill-step")) during a replay. What does patched return, and why?

options.text: true, because the new code is now deployed
options.why: Then old runs would take the new path and break. patched looks at the history, not at the deploy.

options.text: It throws, because old runs cannot run patched code
options.why: Old runs can. That is the whole point of patched: one file serves old and new runs.

options.text: false, because the history has no marker for grill-step
options.why: The marker is written only when a run reaches the line for the first time with the new code. An old history does not have it, so the old path is taken.

check.q: Deploy 1 added patched("grill-step") on Monday. When can deploy 2 replace it with deprecatePatch?

options.text: When no run that started before Monday's deploy is still open
options.why: Only those runs need the old path. A list query on ExecutionStatus and StartTime tells you when they are all closed.

options.text: The next day, because every run has replayed by then
options.why: A run can wait 14 days for a review, and it replays whenever a new worker handles it.

options.text: Right after deploy 1, since patched already wrote the markers
options.why: Runs from before Monday have no marker. With deprecatePatch they would take the new path and break.

p: The orchestrator is deployed while runs are days into their life, so every change to workflow code follows one rule: wrap a new or changed step in patched with an ID that names the change, then deprecatePatch, and delete the line only when no run from before the previous deploy is open. A replay test in CI runs saved histories against every pull request, so a change that would break an open run fails the PR instead of a ticket.

One kind of workflow lives forever: slots, one per agent, which hands out VM slots by signal. It continues as new after 5,000 events and passes its holders and its waiting line along. The Jira polls do not need this, because each tick of a schedule starts a new, short run.

tickets.why: The patching rule for workflow changes and the replay test that guards it in CI.
The slots workflow, which lives forever and continues as new.
The grill step: a new step added at the top of a workflow with open runs.

words.plain: A request the workflow sends to the Temporal Service, such as scheduling an activity or starting a timer.
The worker's refusal to continue a run when the code asks for different steps than the history recorded.
A check that lets old runs take the old path and new runs the new one, using a marker in the history.
The second step of removing a patch: always the new path, but the marker is still written.
Ends the run and starts a fresh one with the same ID and an empty history, passing on only its arguments.

review.q: List the three deploys that take a patch from added to gone, and the condition before deploys 2 and 3.
review.a: 1: patched around the new step. 2: deprecatePatch, once no run from before deploy 1 is open. 3: plain code, once no run from before deploy 2 is open.

review.q: Why does changing the body of the writePlan activity never need a patch?
review.a: Activity code is not replayed. A replay uses the recorded result, and only workflow commands are compared with the history.

review.q: What does slots pass to continueAsNew, and what would happen if it passed nothing?
review.a: The agent, the holders and the waiting line. With nothing, the new run would forget who holds a slot and who waits, and hand out too many VMs or lose requests.

remember: A run can outlive your code: wrap every new step in patched until the old runs are gone, and let a never-ending workflow continue as new.
